steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis when the pruning removes whole layers instead of weights or filters, including finding winning tickets at initialization. Cover background on LTH and its variants, the gap we address, our contributions, and a summary of the main results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Lottery Ticket Hypothesis and what it enables
- Variants: weight rewinding relaxations, structured pruning, practical issue with unstructured pruning
- Categories by when tickets are picked: after, during, before training
- Gap: LTH only prunes small structures; layer removal unexplored
- Contributions
- Summary of results

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- LTH
  - dense (pre-trained) nets contain sparse subnetworks reaching same accuracy when trained from original init of dense counterpart (cite); such tickets = winning tickets
  - advances: cheaper training by replacing dense net with sparse subnetwork during (cite) or before training (cite)
  - adversarial attacks: sparse versions increase robustness (cite)
- Variants
  - traditional: prune weights, reset survivors to original init (cite) = weight rewinding
  - relax rewinding: inherit weights from different training epochs (cite), even random (re)initialization (cite)
  - replace weight pruning (unstructured) with filter pruning (structured) (cite)
  - Prasanna et al. (cite): LHN with structured pruning, removing self-attention heads of multi-head attention (cite)
  - drawback of unstructured: TensorFlow, Pytorch don't support sparse tensor computations; needs specialized frameworks/hardware (Nvidia A100 GPU) (cite)
- Categories by phase
  - after training: train dense, extract subnetwork by importance (pruning) criterion = original LTH (cite)
  - during training: subnetwork when learning is over (cite)
  - before training: pruning at initialization, relatively recent (cite); pick subnetworks using randomly initialized params, no update
  - lots of effort on pruning at init: all benefits of sparsity without training a dense network
- Gap
  - all LTH categories remove small structures (weights, filters)
  - outside LTH: removing entire layers has notable benefits; reduces sequential processing (latency) (cite)
  - many studies remove layers (cite)
  - none for LTH / pruning at initialization
  - we: LTH when pruning removes layers; verify winning tickets exist; systematic strategy to find them before training (layer removal at init matching dense)
- Contributions
  - winning tickets exist with layer removal; more efficient in memory, inference time (latency), carbon emission vs standard LTH pruning (Figure 1)
  - find them at initialization without training; low-cost energy-efficient training; unlike previous LTH studies (cite) no heavy resources for initial over-parameterized dense net
  - share properties with structured LTH (filter pruning), e.g. emerge early in training
  - filter pruning tickets poor on shallow (underparametrized) nets and before training, consistent with prior evidence (cite); hardly become winning tickets; ours easily win -> does eliminated structure matter?
- Results
  - accurate, robust to pruning criteria, density, weight rewinding
  - at init: training up to 2\times faster, notable FLOPs and memory savings
  - one pruning criterion: all tickets beat dense -> all win
  - up to 51\% less carbon emission in training; green AI
  - as suggested by previous works (cite): adversarial images with CIFAR-C (cite), out-of-distribution with CIFAR-10.2 (cite)
  - standard clean training: more robust than dense; safety-critical applications
  - code: https://github.com/arturjordao/LayerLottery

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) conjectures that (pre-trained) dense networks have sparse subnetworks inside them that can get the same accuracy when they are trained from the original initialization of their dense counterpart. Subnetworks (tickets) that have this property are called winning tickets. Many advances came out of the LTH. For example, the computational cost of learning a dense network can be reduced by replacing it with a sparse subnetwork during training or before training. Also, for adversarial attacks, dense networks can be made more robust by considering their sparse versions.

The traditional LTH looks for winning tickets by removing (i.e., pruning) weights of a dense network and setting the surviving weights back to their original initialization, which is called weight rewinding. Some variants of this mechanism relax the weight-rewinding constraint and let subnetworks inherit weights from different training epochs or even from random (re) initialization. Another variant of the traditional LTH replaces weight pruning (unstructured) with filter pruning (structured). For example, Prasanna et al. studied the LHN on structured pruning by removing self-attention modules (i.e., heads from multi-head attention layers). One practical problem with unstructured pruning is that current deep learning frameworks (e.g., TensorFlow and Pytorch) do not support sparse tensor computations. So to get performance gains, this family of pruning needs specialized frameworks or hardware (Nvidia A100 GPU) that optimize sparse computations.

No matter the structure, LTH can be categorized by the phase where the pruning algorithm picks the subnetworks (tickets): after, during, or before training. The first class trains a dense network and then extracts a subnetwork using an importance criterion (pruning criterion), and these steps make up the original LTH. The second class prunes a dense network while it is training, and gets a subnetwork when the learning phase is over. Finally, pruning before training is a relatively recent form of pruning called pruning at initialization. The idea of this category is to find subnetworks before training, which means using the randomly initialized parameters (without any update) to guide the pruning algorithm in picking subnetworks. A lot of effort has gone into pruning at initialization because it gives all the benefits of sparse subnetworks without spending computational resources on training a dense network (which the other categories need).

- Gap
  - all LTH categories remove small structures (weights, filters)
  - outside LTH: removing entire layers has notable benefits; reduces sequential processing (latency) (cite)
  - many studies remove layers (cite)
  - none for LTH / pruning at initialization
  - we: LTH when pruning removes layers; verify winning tickets exist; systematic strategy to find them before training (layer removal at init matching dense)
- Contributions
  - winning tickets exist with layer removal; more efficient in memory, inference time (latency), carbon emission vs standard LTH pruning (Figure 1)
  - find them at initialization without training; low-cost energy-efficient training; unlike previous LTH studies (cite) no heavy resources for initial over-parameterized dense net
  - share properties with structured LTH (filter pruning), e.g. emerge early in training
  - filter pruning tickets poor on shallow (underparametrized) nets and before training, consistent with prior evidence (cite); hardly become winning tickets; ours easily win -> does eliminated structure matter?
- Results
  - accurate, robust to pruning criteria, density, weight rewinding
  - at init: training up to 2\times faster, notable FLOPs and memory savings
  - one pruning criterion: all tickets beat dense -> all win
  - up to 51\% less carbon emission in training; green AI
  - as suggested by previous works (cite): adversarial images with CIFAR-C (cite), out-of-distribution with CIFAR-10.2 (cite)
  - standard clean training: more robust than dense; safety-critical applications
  - code: https://github.com/arturjordao/LayerLottery

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) conjectures that (pre-trained) dense networks have sparse subnetworks inside them that can get the same accuracy when they are trained from the original initialization of their dense counterpart. Subnetworks (tickets) that have this property are called winning tickets. Many advances came out of the LTH. For example, the computational cost of learning a dense network can be reduced by replacing it with a sparse subnetwork during training or before training. Also, for adversarial attacks, dense networks can be made more robust by considering their sparse versions.

The traditional LTH looks for winning tickets by removing (i.e., pruning) weights of a dense network and setting the surviving weights back to their original initialization, which is called weight rewinding. Some variants of this mechanism relax the weight-rewinding constraint and let subnetworks inherit weights from different training epochs or even from random (re) initialization. Another variant of the traditional LTH replaces weight pruning (unstructured) with filter pruning (structured). For example, Prasanna et al. studied the LHN on structured pruning by removing self-attention modules (i.e., heads from multi-head attention layers). One practical problem with unstructured pruning is that current deep learning frameworks (e.g., TensorFlow and Pytorch) do not support sparse tensor computations. So to get performance gains, this family of pruning needs specialized frameworks or hardware (Nvidia A100 GPU) that optimize sparse computations.

No matter the structure, LTH can be categorized by the phase where the pruning algorithm picks the subnetworks (tickets): after, during, or before training. The first class trains a dense network and then extracts a subnetwork using an importance criterion (pruning criterion), and these steps make up the original LTH. The second class prunes a dense network while it is training, and gets a subnetwork when the learning phase is over. Finally, pruning before training is a relatively recent form of pruning called pruning at initialization. The idea of this category is to find subnetworks before training, which means using the randomly initialized parameters (without any update) to guide the pruning algorithm in picking subnetworks. A lot of effort has gone into pruning at initialization because it gives all the benefits of sparse subnetworks without spending computational resources on training a dense network (which the other categories need).

Importantly, all the pruning categories in LTH have the same characteristic: the pruning removes small structures like weights or filters. Outside of LTH, previous works have shown notable benefits from removing entire layers instead of small structures. In particular, this kind of structured pruning gives extra performance gains because it reduces the sequential processing (latency) of a network. So many studies have focused on removing layers instead of other structures. Unfortunately, none of this work has been done in the direction of LTH and pruning at initialization. To bridge this gap, we take a step towards understanding how LTH behaves when the pruning process removes layers. In this setting, we first check that winning tickets exist. Then we propose a systematic strategy for finding winning tickets before training, which means finding sparse subnetworks (from layer removal) at initialization that match the predictive ability of their dense equivalent.

Contributions. Our key contributions are the following. First, we show that winning tickets (sparse subnetworks that get the same accuracy as their dense equivalent) exist when the pruning process removes layers. In practice, this makes winning tickets more efficient in memory consumption, inference time (latency) and carbon emission, because removing layers gives better computational benefits than the standard forms of pruning used in LTH (see Figure 1). Second, we manage to find winning tickets from layer removal at initialization without any training. This helps with low-cost and energy-efficient training, because we can replace learning a dense network with learning its sparse version. Unlike previous LTH studies, this removes the need for heavy computational resources to learn the initial (over-parameterized) dense network. Finally, we show that this new family of subnetworks has some properties of the standard structured LTH (filter pruning), for example, they emerge early in training. On the other hand, we see that subnetworks from filter pruning perform poorly when applied to shallow (underparametrized) networks and before training, which agrees with previous evidence. So tickets from filter pruning hardly become winning tickets. But our tickets (layer removal) easily win the lottery, which raises the question of whether the eliminated structure plays a role in the LTH and pruning at initialization.

Our analysis shows that winning tickets from layer pruning are accurate and robust to many settings like the pruning criteria and density, and weight rewinding. When they are found at initialization, these winning tickets make training up to 2\times faster and save notable FLOPs and memory consumption. With a specific pruning criterion, all tickets do better than their dense counterpart, so all tickets become winning tickets. Also, our winning tickets reduce carbon emission during training by up to 51\%, which is an important step towards democratization and sustainability of Artificial Intelligence (AI), i.e., green AI. Like previous works suggested, we also evaluate our winning tickets on adversarial images and on out-of-distribution examples, using the CIFAR-C and CIFAR-10.2 datasets respectively. With standard clean training (i.e., without any defense mechanism), tickets from layer pruning are more robust than their dense equivalent, which confirms they are suitable for safety-critical applications. For reproducibility, our code is publicly available: https://github.com/arturjordao/LayerLottery.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) conjectures that (pre-trained) dense networks contain sparse subnetworks capable of obtaining the same accuracy when trained from the original initialization of their dense counterpart [1]. Subnetworks (tickets) that satisfy this property are called winning tickets. Many advances have emerged from the LTH; for example, we can reduce the computational cost of learning a dense network by replacing it with a sparse subnetwork during [2,3] or before training [4,5,6]. In the context of adversarial attacks, we can also increase the robustness of dense networks by considering their sparse versions [7,8,9].

The traditional LTH seeks winning tickets by removing (i.e., pruning) weights of a dense network and assigning the surviving weights to their original initialization [1] – weight rewinding. Variants of this mechanism relax the weight-rewinding constraint, enabling subnetworks to inherit weights from different training epochs [10,11] and even from random (re) initialization [12]. Another variant of the traditional LTH replaces weight pruning (unstructured) with filter pruning (structured) [12,11,2]. For example, Prasanna et al. [13] studied the LHN on structured pruning by removing self-attention modules (i.e., heads from multi-head attention layers [14]). One practical drawback of unstructured pruning is that existing deep learning frameworks (e.g., TensorFlow and Pytorch) do not support sparse tensor computations. Hence, to obtain performance gains, this family of pruning requires specialized frameworks or hardware (Nvidia A100 GPU) for optimizing sparse computations [15,16,17].

Regardless of the structure, we can categorize LTH according to the phase in which the pruning algorithm picks the subnetworks (tickets): after, during, or before training. The first class trains a dense network and then extracts a subnetwork according to an importance criterion (pruning criterion); these steps compose the original LTH [1]. The second prunes a dense network during the course of training, obtaining a subnetwork when the learning phase is over [2,3]. Finally, pruning before training is a relatively recent form of pruning named pruning at initialization [4,6,5]. The idea behind this category is to find subnetworks prior to training, using the randomly initialized parameters (without any update) to guide the pruning algorithm. Many efforts have been put into pruning at initialization, as it provides all the benefits of sparse subnetworks without spending computational resources to train a dense network (a process required by the other categories).

Importantly, all pruning categories in LTH share the same characteristic: the pruning eliminates small structures such as weights or filters. Outside the context of LTH, previous works have demonstrated notable benefits of removing entire layers instead of small structures. In particular, this type of structured pruning promotes additional performance gains since it reduces the sequential processing (latency) of a network [18,19]. Hence, many studies have focused on removing layers instead of other structures [20,21,19,22]. Unfortunately, none of these efforts have been made in the direction of LTH and pruning at initialization. To bridge this gap, we take a step towards understanding the behavior of LTH when the pruning process removes layers. In this setting, we first verify the existence of winning tickets. Then, we propose a systematic strategy for discovering winning tickets before training, that is, finding sparse subnetworks (from layer removal) at initialization that match the predictive ability of their dense equivalent.

Contributions. We list the following key contributions. First, we demonstrate the existence of winning tickets – sparse subnetworks that obtain the same accuracy as their dense equivalent – when the pruning process removes layers. From a practical perspective, this enables winning tickets to be more efficient in terms of memory consumption, inference time (latency) and carbon emission, as removing layers provides superior computational benefits compared to the standard forms of pruning employed in LTH (see Figure 1). Second, we successfully find winning tickets from layer removal at initialization without any training. This contribution plays a role in low-cost and energy-efficient training, as we can replace the learning of a dense network with its sparse version. In contrast to previous LTH studies [10,11], it eliminates the need for heavy computational resources to learn the initial (over-parameterized) dense network. Finally, we show that this novel family of subnetworks shares some properties of the standard structured LTH (filter pruning); for example, they emerge early in training. On the other hand, we observe that subnetworks from filter pruning exhibit poor performance when applied to shallow (underparametrized) networks and before training, which is aligned with previous evidence [8]. In other words, tickets from filter pruning hardly become winning tickets. However, our tickets (layer removal) easily win the lottery, raising the question of whether the eliminated structure plays a role in the LTH and pruning at initialization.

According to our analysis, winning tickets from layer pruning are accurate and robust to many settings, such as the pruning criteria and density, and weight rewinding. When found at initialization, these winning tickets speed up training by up to 2\times and save notable FLOPs and memory consumption. On a specific pruning criterion, all tickets outperform their dense counterpart – all tickets become winning tickets. Additionally, our winning tickets reduce carbon emission during training by up to 51\%, an important step towards the democratization and sustainability of Artificial Intelligence (AI) – green AI. As suggested by previous works [8,9,3], we also evaluate our winning tickets on adversarial images and out-of-distribution examples using the CIFAR-C [23] and CIFAR-10.2 [24] datasets, respectively. On standard clean training (i.e., without any defense mechanism), tickets from layer pruning achieve higher robustness than their dense equivalent, confirming their suitability for safety-critical applications. For reproducibility purposes, our code is publicly available: https://github.com/arturjordao/LayerLottery.
